wo8uy7-d1e93-d1e111.summary: Introduces an 'incidental question' to clarify points from the preceding question, the first of several brief questions: whether a property (passio) knowable of a subject by scientia proprie dicta differs really from that subject.

wo8uy7-d1e93-d1e122.summary: Argument for real distinction: according to Metaphysics VI there is no demonstration of substance, so what is demonstrable of something is not really the same as it and hence is really distinct from it.
claims: There is no demonstration of substance.

wo8uy7-d1e93-d1e131.summary: Argument to the contrary: if properties had to be really distinct from their subjects, there could be no scientia proprie dicta about God, since nothing is really distinct from the divine simplicity.
claims: If properties had to be really distinct from subjects, there would be no strict science of God.

wo8uy7-d1e93-d1e142.summary: Sets out an opinion (Scotist in character) that every property is really the same as its subject. Its argument: what is known to inhere necessarily in a subject, so that the opposite includes a contradiction, is really the same as the subject, since anything really distinct and naturally posterior could exist without it. The opinion then gives three ways a property can be knowable of a subject. (1) Formally distinct ex parte rei but not part of its quidditative concept, like unity in relation to being. (2) Distinct only by the intellect, like 'creative' said of God, importing a relation of reason. (3) Not distinct in any of these ways: the divine essence itself causes in a proportioned intellect both a quidditative concept and a real denominative or respective concept such as 'creative', as man naturally expresses the concept of risibility before any intellectual work.
claims: What is known to inhere necessarily in a subject is really the same as the subject (reported view).
A property may be formally distinct from its subject without being really distinct (reported view).
The same formality can ground both a quidditative and a non-quidditative real concept (reported view).
Risibility involves no further absolute thing, accidental relation or relation of reason (reported view).

wo8uy7-d1e93-d1e226.summary: Argues against the first mode of the opinion. A formal distinction with real identity exists only between the divine essence and the relations, where neither is the property of the other. Even if it were possible elsewhere, one item would not be demonstrated of the other: the proposition composed of them would be immediate and self-evident given real identity, and whatever is really one makes a per se unity, so each would belong to the per se understanding of the other. Against the opinion's reply that 'coloredness' is part of the per se concept of whiteness: if coloredness is formally distinct from whiteness, something in whiteness lies outside the concept of coloredness, so one would be the property of the other, which the opponents themselves reject.
claims: Formal distinction with real identity holds only between the divine essence and the relations.
Really identical items would form immediate, self-evident propositions and so would not be demonstrated of one another.
Whatever is really one makes a per se unity.
The opinion's treatment of coloredness and whiteness is internally inconsistent.

wo8uy7-d1e93-d1e278.summary: Confirms the critique: there is no reason why some items that are formally distinct but really one, neither being in the concept of the other, should be related as subject and property rather than form a per se unity, since all such items are equally distinguished. Consistency requires saying this of all or none.
claims: Formally distinct, really identical items are all on a par as to whether they are subject and property.

wo8uy7-d1e93-d1e294.summary: Against the second mode, defers the refutation to a later place, where it will be proved that 'creative' and similar terms do not import a relation of reason.
claims: 'Creative' does not import a relation of reason (to be proved later).

wo8uy7-d1e93-d1e301.summary: Against the third mode: first, it seems self-contradictory. Second, every respective concept necessarily imports some relation, just as an absolute concept imports something absolute. If 'creative' is a respective concept it imports a relation, which on their view is not real and so must be a relation of reason, collapsing the third mode into the second. This is shown from the word 'creative' being relative.
claims: Every respective concept imports some relation.
On the opponents' view, 'creative' must import a relation of reason.

wo8uy7-d1e93-d1e321.summary: A further argument against the third mode, drawing on an earlier proof: there cannot be two concepts of one simple thing with no distinction, a quidditative and a denominative, importing exactly the same thing. So a single thing, prior to any concept of something else, cannot express such a double concept.
claims: One simple thing without any distinction cannot have both a quidditative and a denominative concept importing exactly the same thing.

wo8uy7-d1e93-d1e334.summary: Begins Ockham's answer by distinguishing two senses of 'passio': (1) a thing said to belong to another thing; (2) what is predicated of something per se in the second mode.
claims: 'Passio' signifies either a thing belonging to another thing or a second-mode per se predicate.

wo8uy7-d1e93-d1e344.summary: In the first sense a property is always really distinct from its subject, since it is an accident or form inhering in it, though this is not how the sciences ordinarily use the term. In the second sense a property is never really the same as its subject, because it is a concept predicable of the subject for the thing, not for itself, and a concept is never really the same as what it is a concept of. That the predicated property is a concept follows from nominalist premises: outside the mind there are only singular things, and no singular thing is predicated in 'every man is risible'. If one were, there would be no reason to choose one over another. Also, only what is known to the person forming the proposition is predicated, and not every risible thing is known.
claims: Taken as an inhering thing, a property is always really distinct from its subject.
Taken as a second-mode predicate, a property is a concept predicated for things, not for itself.
A concept is never really the same as that of which it is a concept.
Outside the mind there are only singular things.
Only concepts, not things, are predicated in mental propositions.

wo8uy7-d1e93-d1e386.summary: A further argument from Boethius (On Interpretation) that propositions exist in the mind, in speech and in writing: distinct spoken propositions correspond to distinct mental ones. 'Socrates is risible' and 'Plato is risible' share the same predicate in speech, so also in the mind. But no single undivided thing is predicated of both Socrates and Plato, so the mental predicate is a concept that is verified for one thing in one proposition and for another in the other.
claims: Propositions exist in mind, speech and writing, with distinct spoken propositions corresponding to distinct mental ones.
The same predicate in 'Socrates is risible' and 'Plato is risible' is a concept verified for different things.

wo8uy7-d1e93-d1e410.summary: Qualifies the account: although the property is not really the same as the subject (and on the view that concepts have only objective being, not really distinct either), two items can be related as subject and real property only because they in some way import a real distinction. 'Risible' supposits for man in 'every man is risible' but connotes the act of laughing, primarily or secondarily. The same holds for 'creative' with respect to God, for 'respective properties', and for concrete terms whose abstracts import other things, such as 'hot' and 'cold'.
claims: Subject and property must in some way import a real distinction.
'Risible' supposits for man but connotes the act of laughing.
'Creative' said of God connotes something really distinct from God.

wo8uy7-d1e93-d1e454.summary: Raises objections to the requirement of an imported real distinction: 'corruptible' is a property of composite substance yet seems to import no other thing, and 'eternal', 'infinite', 'immortal' are properties of God.

wo8uy7-d1e93-d1e463.summary: Answers the case of 'corruptible': it imports another thing, at least a part distinct from the whole. Ockham adds that part–whole distinction alone does not make one item a property and the other its subject. The relation holds when the concept also imports the negation, actual or potential, of one part from another, as 'corruptible' imports that one part can be separated from another.
claims: 'Corruptible' imports a part distinct from the whole.
Part–whole distinction alone is not sufficient for a subject–property relation.
The relation holds when actual or potential separation of parts is imported.

wo8uy7-d1e93-d1e485.summary: Answers the divine-attribute case: 'eternal' connotes time, which is really distinct from God, to be explained in Book II. 'Infinite', 'immortal' and similar terms are negative, and every negative concept in some way imports a distinction of things.
claims: 'Eternal' connotes time, which is really distinct from God.
Every negative concept imports some distinction of things.

wo8uy7-d1e93-d1e499.summary: Answers the opposing opinion's first argument, that a property not really the same as its subject could be separated from it. A property that is a thing can indeed be separated and so does not necessarily inhere, but such a property is not demonstrable of the subject. A property in the second sense is neither really the same nor (on one view) really distinct, since it is not a thing. It is demonstrated only to be predicated of the subject for the thing, whether or not the real property inheres, through propositions de possibili or their equivalents ('every man is risible' equals 'every man can laugh'). Hence Ockham concedes that when a property imports a thing apt to inhere, no purely assertoric present-tense proposition is simply necessary.
claims: A separable real property is not what is demonstrated of a subject.
What is demonstrated is the predication of a concept for the thing, through propositions de possibili.
'Every man is risible' is equivalent to 'every man can laugh'.
No purely assertoric present-tense proposition about a property importing an inherent thing is simply necessary.

wo8uy7-d1e93-d1e545.summary: Answers the form of the opposing argument by distinguishing the major premise. 'Being the same' as inherence is incompatible with real identity, so the major is impossible in that sense. As predication where both terms supposit for themselves (simple supposition), the major is true but the minor false, since 'every man is risible' would then absurdly identify one concept with another. Where both terms supposit for things, the minor is true but the major false, since what is necessarily predicated of something need not be it really or formally. The principle that what is naturally prior can exist without what is posterior holds of extramental things but is irrelevant for concepts. Demonstration requires only that the conclusion be necessarily true, whether or not subject and predicate can exist apart.
claims: The major premise is equivocal between inherence and predication.
Necessary predication does not require real or formal identity.
Separability of the prior from the posterior applies to extramental things, not to concepts.
Demonstration requires only that the conclusion be necessarily true.

wo8uy7-d1e93-d1e617.summary: Answers the opinion's claim that risibility is a property with no real, formal, rational or real-relational distinction from man: risibility does imply something really distinct from man. 'Risibility', 'to laugh', 'laughter' and 'risible' share a significate imported primarily or secondarily, and this is why risibility can be a property.
claims: Risibility implies something really distinct from man.
Cognate terms like 'risibility', 'laughter' and 'risible' share a significate.

wo8uy7-d1e93-d1e633.summary: A key semantic diagnosis: asking whether risibility ex parte rei is really or formally distinct from man rests on a 'false imagination' that connotative terms have a quid rei, when they have only a quid nominis. Risibility, aptitude and the like do not signify one thing, either per se or per accidens. Each is equivalent to a complex expression ('risible' equals 'something able to laugh'), and whatever the concrete term imports, its abstract also imports. So one should ask only what 'risibility' signifies, not what it is in reality. Strictly speaking, nothing that signifies exactly one thing can be truly predicated with such an abstract, as with 'this is blindness'.
claims: Connotative terms have only a nominal definition (quid nominis), not a real definition (quid rei).
Abstract connotative terms like 'risibility' do not signify one thing in reality.
A connotative term is equivalent to a complex expression.
One should ask what such terms signify, not what they are.

wo8uy7-d1e93-d1e709.summary: Answers the objection that blindness is merely privative and so a poor example. Privations and negations signify only positive things or concepts and are not separately conceivable entities: 'blindness' signifies an eye unable to see. Further examples follow. 'Creativity' is predicated of no single thing, neither God nor creature, but signifies the whole 'something that can produce from nothing'. 'Potentiality of matter' signifies no absolute thing, real relation or relation of reason, but that matter can have a form it lacks. Many arguments commit the fallacy of figure of speech by treating connotative names as absolute ones, for instance 'whatever God can do through a secondary cause he can do immediately; he produces a meritorious act through an act of will; so he can produce it without one'.
claims: Privations and negations signify only positive things or concepts.
'Creativity' is not predicable of any one thing.
The potentiality of matter is neither an absolute thing nor a relation.
Treating connotative names as absolute produces the fallacy of figure of speech.

wo8uy7-d1e93-d1e766.summary: Notes that abstracts like 'risibility' and 'aptitude' are used equivocally by Aristotle: sometimes they supposit for what their concretes supposit for, so 'risibility is man' would be true, and sometimes for an aggregate of everything they import, primarily or secondarily.
claims: Abstract terms like 'risibility' are used equivocally in Aristotle.
In one usage 'risibility is man' is true.

wo8uy7-d1e93-d1e785.summary: Draws consequences: a denominative concept predicable in the second mode is not caused solely by the thing it is predicated of, prior to any other concept. It presupposes concepts of whatever it imports, so 'creative' cannot be had without knowing something other than God. It is also wrong to say one thing is subject under one concept and property under another, because the concept itself is the property. Ockham then raises opposing authorities: Aristotle's Topics distinguishes property from definition as accident from quid, and Grosseteste says that in first-mode predication the subject's quiddity proceeds from the predicate's and the reverse in the second, implying real distinction of subject and predicate.
claims: A denominative second-mode concept presupposes concepts of what it imports.
The concept 'creative' cannot be had without knowing something other than God.
The concept, not the thing under a concept, is the property.

wo8uy7-d1e93-d1e824.summary: Confirms the objection from Grosseteste: according to him there is no mode of per se predication unless the subject is the cause of the predicate or the reverse.

wo8uy7-d1e93-d1e833.summary: Answers the Topics authority: Aristotle there means by 'accident' anything extrinsic to the thing, as opposed to quid. A proprium always imports something extrinsic and is convertible. So 'creative' is truly a proprium of God because it is convertible with God and imports creatures really distinct from God, though it signifies no accident in God.
claims: In the Topics 'accident' means whatever is extrinsic, as opposed to quid.
'Creative' is a proprium of God without signifying an accident in God.

wo8uy7-d1e93-d1e851.summary: Answers the Grosseteste authority: the predicate need not be distinct from the subject or a real effect of it. It suffices that something imported by the subject causes something imported by the predicate, in true, proper, affirmative second-mode predication, extending 'cause' to integral parts, which are in a way causes of the whole. This also answers the confirmation.
claims: Second-mode per se predication requires only that something imported by the subject cause something imported by the predicate.
Integral parts can count as causes of the whole.

wo8uy7-d1e93-d1e873.summary: Answers the principal argument by denying the inference 'what is demonstrable of something is not really the same as it, so it is really distinct from it'. A counterexample is a being of reason, which on the view that posits objective beings of reason in the soul is neither really the same as a thing nor really distinct from it.
claims: Not being really the same does not entail being really distinct.
A being of reason is neither really identical to nor really distinct from a thing (on the objective-being view).

wo8uy7-d1e93.summary: Prologue question 3, an 'incidental question' clarifying the previous question, asks whether a property knowable of a subject by scientia proprie dicta differs really from it. Ockham rejects a Scotist-style opinion that properties are really identical with their subjects, whether through formal distinction, a distinction of reason, or a real non-quidditative concept. He argues that formal distinction with real identity holds only in the Trinity, that really identical items would form immediate rather than demonstrable propositions, and that one simple thing cannot ground two such concepts. His own answer distinguishes 'passio' as an inhering thing, which is always really distinct, from 'passio' as a second-mode predicate. The latter is a concept predicated for things, never really identical to them, as shown from nominalist premises and Boethius's mental language. Subject and property must still import a real distinction through connotation ('risible' connotes laughing, 'creative' connotes creatures, 'eternal' connotes time). The central semantic diagnosis is that connotative abstracts like 'risibility', 'creativity' or 'potentiality of matter' have only a quid nominis and signify no single thing. Treating them as absolute terms causes the fallacy of figure of speech. Demonstration concerns necessary propositions de possibili about concepts, not separability of things.
claims: A property as a second-mode predicate is a concept, never really identical with its subject.
Subject and property must import some real distinction through connotation.
Connotative abstract terms have only a quid nominis and do not signify single entities.
Formal distinction with real identity is found only between the divine essence and the relations.
Necessary propositions about properties are de possibili or equivalent to them.
